newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN TABLES NEW PROPOSALS AT DEADLOCKED CYPRUS TALKS.
newsitem.headline: UN TABLES NEW PROPOSALS AT DEADLOCKED CYPRUS TALKS.

text.p: The U.N. mediator at the deadlocked Cyprus talks in Switzerland has submitted new proposals to Greek and Turkish Cypriot leaders in an effort to overcome the impasse, officials close to the negotiations said on Wednesday.

They said U.N. special Cyprus envoy Diego Cordovez submitted two working papers to Glafcos Clerides and Rauf Dentash on Tuesday and asked them to present their views at a meeting planned for Wednesday.

The five-day talks, which began on Monday at a hotel in the village of Glion near Montreux, have been stalled amid total disagreement over the key issues of sovereignty, resettlement of refugees, security and guarantor states.
The same issues have for decades deadlocked efforts to reunite the Mediterranean island under a bi-zonal, bi-communal federation.
Officials from both sides declined comment on the contents of the new Cordovez proposals because of a news blackout.
Clerides, president of the internationally-recognised Greek Cypriot government in the divided capital Nicosia, only confirmed receiving the documents.
He said as he left a three-hour meeting with Greek Cypriot politicians that he was studying the documents.
In a sign of the importance he attached to the papers, he told reporters: "It is a serious time we are going through."

Hours before, Denktash had warned he was not prepared to agree to any joint declaration or sign a framework accord sought by Cordovez at the end of the Glion talks. "I hope he does not insist," Denktash told reporters.
Denktash has repeatedly said he will reject any document placed on the table before he is consulted on its contents.

Officials said the latest proposals were contained in a draft document on the procedure of the talks, including a timetable, and an annex document mostly about a proposed constitution and also referring to key issues about Cyprus.
They incorporated some of Cordovez's observations from meetings with the two sides, the officials said.
Diplomats close to the talks noted that the latest drafts were an amended and lighter version of proposals submitted by Cordovez to Clerides and Denktash in New York.

Those proposals, a so-called non-document which the pair took home for further study, were no longer on the table because of deep divisions, and the new, amended version could face a similar fate in the deadlocked talks, they said.

Denktash says he will pull out of the negotiations unless the European Union shelves plans for starting talks about admitting Cyprus to the bloc. The Greek Cypriots say the issue of EU membership has nothing to do with the talks.
Another major sticking point is Turkish Cypriot insistence on sovereign equality, anathema to Greek Cypriots who point out that Turkish Cypriots make up just 18 percent of the island population.
Cyprus has been divided since 1974 when Turkey invaded its northern third after a coup in Nicosia engineered by the military junta then ruling Greece.
The two communities have been estranged since 1963 when a government in which both took part broke down amid violence, three years after independence from Britain.
